name: Muqaddimah
info: The Muqaddimah is a 14th-century Arabic treatise on historiography, sociology and the philosophy of history by Ibn Khaldun, written in 1377 as the introduction to his world history, the Kitab al-ʿIbar, and read as a work in its own right.

facts.made: Ibn Khaldun, who wrote it at Qalʿat ibn Salama after withdrawing from political life, as the introduction and first book of his planned world history, the Kitab al-ʿIbar
facts.form: An Arabic treatise in six books on society, politics, urban life, economics and knowledge, with discussions of historiography, theology and the natural sciences; the Kitab al-ʿIbar it introduces fills seventeen volumes of 500 pages each in its modern edition
facts.where: Read in printed editions and in translations into Ottoman Turkish, French and English; manuscripts copied in Ibn Khaldun's lifetime survive, some with his own marginal notes or additions
facts.known: The ʿasabiyyah cycle of dynasties; the new science of ʿumrān; a criticism of the errors of historians; the contrast of nomadic and sedentary life; passages on taxation and prices; the discussion of alchemy

t: Ibn Khaldun wrote it in 1377 as the introduction to a universal history, and it came to be regarded as an independent work in his own lifetime.
It sets out a new science of human society, ʿilm al-ʿumrān, and explains the rise and fall of dynasties through ʿasabiyyah, or group feeling.
It was received without much enthusiasm for centuries, first printed in Cairo in 1857, and translated into French in 1863 and English in 1958.
dyk: Ibn Khaldun wrote that when officials were questioned about armies, or the goods of the wealthy were assessed, the true figures would be found to amount to a tenth of what those people had said.
ev: Ibn Khaldun completes a draft of the Muqaddimah at Qalʿat ibn Salama
The Muqaddimah is printed at the Bulaq Press in Cairo in a standalone volume
Étienne-Marc Quatremère prints the Arabic text in three volumes in Paris
The complete Ottoman Turkish translation is published, in 1860 or 1861
William McGuckin de Slane publishes a French translation in three volumes
Franz Rosenthal publishes an English translation

sections.origins:
The Muqaddimah is a 14th-century Arabic treatise on historiography, sociology and the philosophy of history by Ibn Khaldun. He wrote it in 1377 as the introduction and first book of a planned work of world history, the Kitab al-ʿIbar, the "Book of Lessons", whose full title promises a record of the beginnings and events in the history of the Arabs, the foreigners and the Berbers and their powerful contemporaries. The word muqaddimah means a prologue or introduction to a larger work.

Ibn Khaldun wrote the first version at Qalʿat ibn Salama, where he secluded himself for almost four years after withdrawing from political life. The Muqaddimah is the first of three parts of a project on which he worked for almost thirty years. Its starting point was a criticism of the historians before him. He named seven critical issues: that all records are liable to error, partisanship towards a creed or opinion, over-confidence in one's sources, the failure to understand what is intended, a mistaken belief in the truth, the inability to place an event in its real context, and the desire to win the favour of the highly placed by praising them. The most important, he wrote, was ignorance of the laws governing the transformation of human society, and against that point he set out his own theory of society.
sections.content:
Sati' al-Husri suggested that the Muqaddimah is essentially a sociological work, sketching over its six books a general sociology, a sociology of politics, of urban life, of economics and of knowledge. Some modern thinkers view it as the first work dealing with the social sciences of sociology, demography and cultural history. It also deals with Islamic theology, historiography, the philosophy of history, economics, political theory and ecology.

Its best known idea is ʿasabiyyah, a word for tribalism or clanism that in a modern context is rendered as group feeling, social cohesion or solidarity. Ibn Khaldun argued that each dynasty carries the seeds of its own downfall. Ruling houses tend to emerge on the peripheries of great empires and use the unity of those areas to change the leadership. Once settled at the centre, the new rulers become lax and concerned with their lifestyles, and a new dynasty may emerge at the periphery and begin the cycle again. He held that civilisations have lifespans like individuals, and that injustice, such as overtaxing and the violation of property rights, ruins civilisation. His framework contrasts nomadic life (badāwa) with sedentary life (ḥaḍāra). On economics he wrote that labour is the source of value, that prices result from supply and demand, and that taxation yields a large revenue from small assessments at the beginning of a dynasty and a small revenue from large assessments at its end.
sections.making:
Ibn Khaldun expounded in the Muqaddimah a "new science" about which he had maintained secrecy until his retirement to Qalʿat ibn Salama. It studies what he called ʿumrān, and he named it ʿilm al-ʿumrān. The science was based on Greco-Arab philosophy and sought to study the evolution of humankind and society throughout history by a method that was essentially historical, empirical, rational and demonstrative. He often criticised "idle superstition and uncritical acceptance of historical data", and presented the new science as something new to his age.

A draft of the Muqaddimah was completed in 1377. It stands as the first part of the Kitab al-ʿIbar, a work of universal history that fills seventeen volumes of 500 pages each in its modern edition. Manuscripts of the Muqaddimah copied in Ibn Khaldun's lifetime survive, and a number of them carry marginal notes or additions in his own hand. In his own lifetime the Muqaddimah was already regarded as an independent work.

His method appears in his treatment of numbers. In the Introduction he criticised the historian al-Masudi for the report that Moses counted an Israelite army of 600,000 or more, and asked whether Egypt and Syria could have held so many soldiers, or whether such an army could march or fight as a unit. He set beside it the Sasanian army at the Battle of al-Qādisiyyah, which he put at 120,000 at most.
sections.reception:
The Muqaddimah, shaped by Ibn Khaldun's characteristic moderation in politics and religion, was met without much enthusiasm or clear hostility in the first few centuries after it was written. Two Moroccan writers alluded to it. Muḥammad b. ʿAlī Ibn al-Azraq, who died in 1496, is apparently the only contemporary writer of the Maghreb who clearly approved of it, and he quoted it abundantly. It was cited more often in Egypt, where disciples including Al-Maqrizi celebrated it and others such as Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani met it with hostility. Biographical dictionaries, among them al-Maqqari's Nafḥ al-ṭīb, described Ibn Khaldun as an authority on political history, but the Muqaddimah itself remained largely absent from them.

Ottoman historians including Kâtip Çelebi and Mustafa Naima valued its social and political theories but did not apply them in the analysis of their own society. Abdesselam Cheddadi concludes that its strictly scientific contribution to the field of history and the social sciences was not fully recognised in the Muslim world until the late nineteenth century.

Its treatment of other peoples drew later criticism. Historians have challenged its classification of the scholars of the Islamic East as non-Arabs, and Abdelmajid Hannoum holds that de Slane's translation misread Ibn Khaldun's distinctions between Berbers and Arabs as a general racial ideology. His remarks on sub-Saharan Africans rest on a theory of climatic determinism, and he applied the same reasoning to explain the enslavement of peoples of the deep south.
sections.survival:
The Muqaddimah was copied in manuscript, and copies made in Ibn Khaldun's lifetime are extant, a number of them with autographed marginal notes or additions. It remained largely absent from the biographical dictionaries that praised its author in the following centuries. Its first printing came in 1857, at the Bulaq Press in Cairo, in a standalone volume prepared by Naṣr al-Hūrīnī with crucial support from Rifa'a at-Tahtawi. A decade later it appeared as the first volume of a seven-volume set of the Kitab al-ʿIbar.

Its route to readers in France ran partly through Turkish. The first five of its six chapters were translated into Ottoman Turkish by Mehmed Pirizade, who died in 1749, and the sixth by Ahmed Cevdet, who died in 1895; the complete translation was published in 1860 or 1861. The work was first discovered in France through Pirizade's partial Turkish translation. In 1858, the year after the Cairo printing, Étienne-Marc Quatremère printed the Arabic text in three volumes in Paris as Les Prolégomènes d'Ebn Khaldoun. William McGuckin de Slane published a French translation in three volumes in 1863, which Aziz al-Azmeh regards as the best translation of the text. Franz Rosenthal published an English translation in 1958.
sections.legacy:
The Muqaddimah is held to be a foundational work for historiography, cultural history and the philosophy of history. Dawood called it the earliest attempt by any historian to discover a pattern in the changes in man's political and social organisation, and an almost complete departure from traditional historiography. Franz Rosenthal wrote that Muslim historiography made a definite advance in the sociological understanding of history and the systematisation of historiography.

Modern readers have compared its ideas with later ones. Its account of ʿasabiyyah has often been compared with Keynesian economics, and its remark on taxes has been read as anticipating supply-side economics and the Laffer curve, which Laffer does not claim to have invented, noting that the idea was present in the work of Ibn Khaldun. Some commentators see in a passage on the ascent from minerals to plants, animals and man an anticipation of biological evolution. Shoaib Ahmed Malik argues instead that the passage belongs to the medieval great chain of being, a graded hierarchy and not a temporal process in which one species originates from another. Ernest Gellner considered Ibn Khaldun's definition of government, an institution which prevents injustice other than such as it commits itself, the best in the history of political philosophy.

summary: The Muqaddimah is Ibn Khaldun's Arabic treatise of 1377 on history and society, written as the introduction to his Kitab al-ʿIbar. It sets out a new science of ʿumrān and the cycle of ʿasabiyyah, and reached wide readerships through printing and translation from 1857.
references: Franz Rosenthal, The Muqaddimah: An Introduction to History, three volumes (Princeton University Press, 1969)
